sentences.text: Roxochampsa was an extinct crocodyliform belonging to the itasuchid family, characterized by a flattened skull with narrow, elongated jaws.
Its teeth featured prominent ridges that formed secondary cutting edges alongside main ridges, creating a pseudo-ziphodont structure.
The lower jaw displays two distinct waves in side view and expands outward at a 25 degree angle to form a narrow Y shape.
This animal possessed nineteen teeth in each half of its lower jaw, with the front ones pointing forward in a sub-horizontal orientation.
Researchers estimate the minimum lower jaw length was 25 centimeters, while the total body size likely reached between one and two meters.
Fossil evidence includes bite marks on a sauropod dinosaur that match modern crocodilian feeding traces rather than those of theropods or mammals.
Fossils of this species have been discovered in the Adamantina and Presidente Prudente Formations within Brazil's Bauru Group.
Teeth similar to this animal were recognized from the region as early as 1911, with specific specimens recovered near Amandaba city in 1935.
New jaw material was described from the Presidente Prudente Formation in 2018, leading to the naming of the genus by Piacentini Pinheiro and colleagues.
Evidence from jaw scars suggests the animal possessed interlocking dentition similar to modern crocodiles, adapted to stab and crush prey rather than impale it.
It was likely a semi-aquatic predator with a generalist diet including fish, turtles, hard-shelled animals, and small to mid-sized terrestrial vertebrates.
The jaw strength was likely sufficient to crack shells of molluscs, crabs, and turtles, while crenulated ridges may have aided in slicing prey or strengthening enamel.
Evidence for the death rolling behavior seen in modern crocodiles is absent in this species and remains unconfirmed in its relatives.
Roxochampsa belongs to the family Itasuchidae, and the type species of the genus is Roxochampsa paulistanus.
Some similar teeth were once referred to the family Trematochampsidae, but recent studies have recovered nearly identical evolutionary groupings despite applying different family names.
The animal lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
The environment featured meandering rivers, sandy bars, and floodplains under an arid to semi-arid climate.
Researchers warn that tooth crowns alone are insufficient for recognizing specific clades or species without substantial fossil remains.
A semi-strict consensus analysis suggests that Roxochampsa and Amargasuchus may be sister taxa, though this remains a hypothesis to resolve phylogenetic uncertainty.
